title: Event Burst Trigger: An Availability Backdoor Attack on Event-Based SNN Object Detection.
abstract: Event-based vision and spiking neural networks (SNNs) are increasingly adopted for edge intelligence under strict latency and energy constraints. However, the vulnerability of event-based SNN object detection models to availability backdoor attacks remains insufficiently studied. This paper presents Event Burst Trigger (EBT), an availability backdoor attack targeting SNN-based object detection models. EBT injects carefully crafted event-based triggers into the training data, which induce temporally concentrated event streams during inference. These burst-like activations increase the number of phantom (i.e., spurious) object candidates, and consequently inflate the computational cost of the post-processing stage, particularly Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS). We evaluate EBT on SpikeYOLO, the state-of-the-art SNN-based object detector, under a poison-only threat model that does not require modifications to the model architecture, loss function, or inference pipeline. Experimental results show that while detection accuracy remains largely preserved, with mAP@0.5 decreasing by less than 0.099, the latency of the NMS stage increases by up to 38%. This indicates that NMS can become a dominant availability bottleneck in event-based SNN object detection. Experiments on an edge platform further show that the proposed attack elevates baseline resource utilization and reduces scheduling slack without inducing conspicuous peaks in resource usage. In addition, STRIP-based backdoor detection fails to reliably distinguish the proposed attack from benign inputs. These results characterize a previously underexplored availability backdoor threat in event-based SNN object detection systems.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: From MIRAGE to CLEAR: Component-Level Explainable Anomaly Reasoning for Autonomous Vehicle Perception Systems.
abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) perception systems remain vulnerable to failures that current anomaly detectors can flag but cannot trace to a specific component; an attribution gap that impedes forensics and emerging transparency mandates like the EU AI Act. We introduce a unified framework comprising MIRAGE and CLEAR. MIRAGE (MUTCD-Informed Realistic Anomalous Generation Engine) integrates 48,022 real-world driving scenes from nuScenes, Waymo Open, and Argoverse 2 with structured rules from the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), generating 5,847 annotated anomalous scenarios with known module-level ground truth across four violation types: direct, subtle, contextual, and environmental. This data powers CLEAR, a hierarchical three-layer LLM pipeline that detects anomalies, classifies violations, and attributes failures to Traffic Sign Recognition (TSR), Automated Lane Centering (ALC), or Object Detection (OD) with interpretable justifications. Confidence-gated propagation and schema-constrained outputs prevent error cascades and minimize hallucinations. CLEAR achieves 95.2% detection accuracy, 62.3% classification accuracy, and 84% attribution accuracy on direct TSR violations. A Top-2 evaluation paired with per-module confidence analysis raises overall attribution to 74.6%, confirming that apparent misattributions largely reflect the multi-module nature of anomaly types rather than reasoning failures. These results show that grounding LLM reasoning in structured traffic regulations enables reliable, interpretable forensics for AV perception systems, offering a practical path toward auditable, regulation-compliant safety analysis. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/David-FR/MIRAGE_CLEAR.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Decentralized Root Cause Analysis for Cloud-Native Microservices - Experience with Distributed PageRank in Production.
abstract: Root cause analysis in microservice systems typically relies on centralized telemetry aggregation, which becomes a bottleneck as deployments scale. We present an architecture that removes the central component entirely: each microservice runs a sidecar diagnostic agent that computes a local anomaly score and participates in gossip-based distributed Personalized PageRank over the service dependency graph. On the RCAEval benchmark (735 failure cases, 12-64 services), Top-1 accuracy is 94.7%, statistically indistinguishable from centralized PageRank at 94.1%, with roughly a third lower diagnosis latency and 74.5% less network traffic. We deployed the system for four weeks on a 15-node AWS EKS cluster handling 1% of live ecommerce traffic. The deployment processed 112 injected faults$(\mathbf{9 4. 6 \%}$Top-1) and 3 organic incidents$(\mathbf{1}$of 3 correct). The production experience exposed problems that benchmarks do not expose: cross-availability-zone gossip asymmetry causing split-brain diagnoses, inadequate global anomaly thresholds, and external-dependency blind spots. We also ran into operational issues we had not anticipated, such as log volume from agents overwhelming the existing logging pipeline.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: An IPsec Tunnel Recovery Protocol to Overcome QKD Key Desynchronization.
abstract: Modern cryptographic systems face increasing threats from quantum computing. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) offers a promising defense by enabling quantum-secure key exchange. Recently, QKD has been integrated with conventional key-exchange protocols to derive final encryption keys for secure networks. However, vulnerabilities in QKD devices-such as key exposure, depletion, or synchronization failures-can propagate to QKD-dependent cryptographic services, leading to plaintext leakage or service disruption. The standard IKEv2 protocol lacks mechanisms to detect or recover from such incidents. This paper presents the QRIKE (Quantum-Resistant IKEv2) protocol, which integrates QKD devices into IKEv2, detects key-synchronization failures, and restores IPsec VPN tunnels via an IKE SA rollback mechanism. In experiments with 1,000 tunnels carrying 3 Gbps of IPsec traffic, encryptors without QRIKE support suffered about 40% throughput degradation, whereas QRIKE maintained all tunnels and processed encrypted traffic stably without disruption, demonstrating strong resilience under quantum-era threats.

title: Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks for EEG-Based Sleep Stage Classification in Noiseless and Noisy Scenarios.
abstract: Sleep disorders affect about one billion people worldwide, yet automated sleep staging is limited by class imbalance in polysomnographic datasets and the representational capacity of classical generative models. This work compares a classical Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) with two Quantum Wasserstein GAN-GP (QWGAN-GP) variants—noiseless and noisy simulator—for synthetic EEG augmentation in sleep stage classification using the ANPHY-Sleep dataset [1]. Models are trained under a Wasserstein GAN with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) across subsets of 2–4 statistical EEG features over 50 epochs. Results show consistent quantum-enhanced variance matching: QWGAN-GP variants achieve lower standard deviation mean absolute error (StdMAE) than the classical GAN, with reductions up to 70.9% at 3 features. The 6-qubit generator (26= 64-dimensional Hilbert space) captures EEG variance more faithfully than a classical multilayer perceptron. Moderate Gaussian noise (σ = 0.1) during QGAN training acts as implicit regularisation, yielding the best StdMAE (0.064) and competitive classification (Accuracy = 0.880, F1 = 0.880). The classical GAN suffers mode collapse at higher dimensions, dropping to 0.535–0.585 accuracy, while the noiseless QGAN reaches 0.905 at 3 features. A downstream classification evaluation on real PSG labels confirms that the quantum generator preserves N1 minority-class F1 (up to 0.1053 at 4 features) where the classical GAN consistently collapses to N1 F1 = 0.000 across all feature configurations. These results demonstrate that hybrid quantum-classical generative models provide a structurally distinct and empirically superior approach for minority-class distribution learning in imbalanced clinical time-series, albeit with higher classical simulation overhead.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Trust Without Safeguards: A Red-Teaming Study of ProteinMPNN in Open Protein Design Pipelines.
abstract: Generative protein design models such as ProteinMPNN enable rapid and accurate sequence generation conditioned on target structures, but their open availability raises dual-use concerns. We present a red-teaming, system-level evaluation of ProteinMPNN under unconstrained usage. Using a sensitive protein (human prion, 1HJM) and a control (1BDD), we generate sequences across sampling conditions and evaluate outputs using sequence metrics and AlphaFold confidence scores. We find that ProteinMPNN consistently produces structurally plausible sequences (pLDDT 0.70–0.84) despite low sequence similarity to native proteins (recovery 0.15–0.30), demonstrating a decoupling between sequence identity and structural outcomes. When combined with downstream validation, this behavior yields high-confidence outputs without enforcing meaningful biological or safety constraints. In open deployment settings, however, this capability enables the generation of plausible variants of sensitive proteins under unconstrained conditions. We characterize this as a dependability gap and highlight the need for safeguards in generative bio-AI systems.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Fault-tolerant and Self-recovering Sharing of Multicast Transmission.
abstract: Multicast transmission is a fundamental operation in overlay networks, enabling efficient data delivery from a source to multiple receivers via a logical tree. However, maintaining such overlays incurs a transmission cost at intermediate nodes, requiring fair cost sharing to prevent selfish behavior and ensure sustainability. Existing approaches address either fault tolerance or economic fairness, but not both, leaving multicast overlays vulnerable to faults or strategic manipulation.We present a fault-tolerant algorithm for multicast overlays that jointly ensures structural recovery and faithful cost sharing. Following transient faults that do not corrupt cryptographic keys, the algorithm autonomously reconstructs a correct multicast tree while distributing transmission costs using a Shapley-based mechanism. Lightweight cryptographic proofs enforce strategyproofness and prevent manipulation. We formally prove convergence, budget balance, and resistance to selfish deviations. Simulations on overlays demonstrate rapid recovery, low steady-state overhead, and robust fairness under adversarial conditions. Our results bridge fault tolerance and economic incentives in multicast overlay systems.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: A Dependability Profile for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Systems.
abstract: Hybrid quantum–classical computing is a key paradigm for executing quantum algorithms on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. However, the dependability of quantum–classical workflows under realistic system conditions remains underexplored. These workflows often involve heterogeneous resources, including CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and cloud-accessible QPUs, introducing variability, resource constraints, and trust concerns. In this work, we propose a methodology for benchmarking the dependability of quantum–classical workflows and their execution on hybrid systems. Our methodology involves establishing a dependability profile for workloads and corresponding systems using empirical measurements and evaluations of standard metrics of speed, scalability, and security of the overall system. Experimental evaluation includes two variational algorithms as case studies deployed on a hybrid CPU–FPGA system with QPU emulation backends that replicate the noise characteristics and gate sets of real quantum processors. For the dependability profile, we define iteration-level metrics for speed: variance, jitter, worst-case latency, stability, and resource-aware scalability metrics: Circuit Layer Operations Per Second (CLOPS). Results demonstrate that the proposed dependability profile enables practical decision-making by linking system behavior to deployability and performance limitations.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Computationally Efficient Anomaly Detection and Exclusion for Practical and Robust Federated Learning.
abstract: We introduce a practical anomaly detection and exclusion algorithm in Federated Learning (FL), titled PID-MADE (Proportional-Integral-Derivative Model Anomaly Detection and Exclusion from aggregation). Inspired by the PID structure, our algorithm enhances robustness and security in FL by accumulating clients’ model deviation history and precisely detecting and excluding anomalies. Contrary to existing defenses, PID-MADE maintains a lightweight computational complexity of O(nd), where n is the number of clients and d is the dimensionality of the model parameter space. PID-MADE’s simple structure makes it easily deployable, without relying on impractical assumptions, such as root-of-trust datasets or prior knowledge of attacker counts. We analyze existing attack models and show theoretically that employing anomaly detection mechanisms in FL provably accelerates convergence. Furthermore, we provide theoretically-grounded recommendations for setting and tuning hyperparameters of our method in practice. Our empirical investigations, conducted across various domains, datasets, model architectures, and attack types, show that PID-MADE not only converges faster than common baselines, but also provides superior attack detection and mitigation, achieving 50× lower server-side computation time compared to the next fastest robust baseline, while reducing the attack success rates by as much as 34% in some cases, highlighting the robustness, security and efficiency enhancement. This paper demonstrates that adoption of anomaly detection and exclusion algorithms is indispensable for practical dependable FL deployments.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Knowledge Transfer from LLMs to Provenance Analysis: Semantic-Augmented APT Detection.
abstract: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) have caused significant losses across a wide range of sectors, including the theft of sensitive data and harm to system integrity. As attack techniques grow increasingly sophisticated and stealthy, the arms race between cyber defenders and attackers continues to intensify. The revolutionary impact of Large Language Models (LLMs) has opened up numerous opportunities in various fields, including cybersecurity. An intriguing question arises: can the extensive knowledge embedded in LLMs be harnessed for provenance analysis and play a positive role in identifying previously unknown malicious events? To seek a deeper understanding of this issue, we propose a new strategy for taking advantage of LLMs in provenance-based APT detection. In our design, the state-of-the-art LLM offers additional details in provenance data interpretation, leveraging their knowledge of system calls, software identity, and high-level understanding of application execution context. The advanced contextualized embedding capability is further utilized to capture the rich semantics of event descriptions. We conducted an empirical analysis of how LLMs interpret system events and obtained multiple insightful findings. We also verified through comparison that the contextualized embeddings generated by LLMs for provenance data outperform existing counterparts. Finally, our evaluation using real-world data shows that supervised threat detection achieves a precision of 99.0%, and semi-supervised anomaly detection attains a precision of 96.9%. The findings suggest that LLMs play a positive role in provenance-based APT detection and demonstrate promising potential for future applications in this area.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Establishing Zero-Shot LLM Performance at Network Tomography.
abstract: This paper investigates the zero-shot capabilities of LLMs to reconstruct the origin network’s underlying structure from the produced NetFlow data. We conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis of thirteen open-weight models and a closed-weight, large-scale model, evaluating their ability to reconstruct topological and application-level features from limited NetFlow samples. We demonstrate that off-the-shelf LLMs can infer certain topological features from NetFlow metadata. However, we identify a clear boundary to these capabilities: while structural inference is strong, models struggle to generate plausible values for dynamic, unbounded numerical features. This study provides a critical baseline for LLM-based traffic analysis, highlighting the fragility of metadata anonymisation and the security implications of deploying LLMs in network-aware applications.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Hi-Fi Flow: Real-Time High-Granularity Flow Feature Extraction for Robust Network Monitoring.
abstract: Modern networks exhibit rapidly expanding traffic volume, diversity, and dynamism, which hinder accurate flow reconstruction and real-time monitoring. Existing flow feature extraction tools primarily rely on static 5-tuple attributes and post-completion processing, resulting in fragmented flow records and delayed detection under evasive behaviors such as IP spoofing, port rotation, and multi-session tunneling. We present Hi-Fi Flow, a real-time, high-granularity flow identification and feature extraction tool that jointly models spatial, temporal, and structural correlations among packets. Hi-Fi Flow employs a dual self-attention encoder to capture complementary endpoint-level and behavior-level dependencies for fine-grained packet-to-flow association. To reduce labeling overhead, it further adopts a few-shot triplet learning strategy that learns discriminative packet-flow similarity patterns with limited labeled data. Extensive evaluations demonstrate near-perfect flow identification accuracy, reaching 99~100% with only 50 labeled samples per attack, and show that Hi-Fi Flow features consistently outperform legacy flowmeters in downstream attack detection tasks. The proposed framework provides an efficient and robust foundation for next-generation network monitoring and threat detection.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Automated Resilience Assessment for Autonomous Systems Using System-on-Chip Architectures.
abstract: In autonomous systems, consolidating hardware onto System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms provides size, weight, and power advantages, yet creates new attack surfaces where a single component’s compromise can propagate attacks across the shared bus to other safety-critical functions. Existing SoC security analyses focus on implementing access controls and system-level anomaly detection algorithms, but lack systematic methods for evaluating how these architectures degrade when compromised. This research introduces an automated resilience assessment that takes an SoC architecture model with pre-assigned security features and systematically generates component failure and compromise scenarios, computes structural and firewall-aware blast radii (the set of components reachable from a compromised node), detects single points of failure (SPOFs), quantifies risk amplification factors based on the blast radii, and enumerates multi-hop attack paths to safety-critical targets. The assessment is formulated in Answer Set Programming (ASP). It is evaluated on two case studies: an 8-component SoC drone and an 11-component DARPA Cyber Assured Systems Engineering (CASE) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The assessment runs in under 15 seconds for the 8-component architecture and under 30 seconds for the CASE UAV, for these two case studies. Results show that topology-driven weaknesses (policy server concentration, common-mode bus failures, and single-string service chains) persist across distinctly different security architectures, suggesting that some weaknesses cannot be removed by per-component hardening alone. The accompanying formal metric definitions enable systematic comparison across architectures and security postures.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: From Security Standards to Adversary Emulation: An AI-Assisted Framework for ICS Security Assessment.
abstract: Security assessments are essential to ensure that Industrial Control Systems (ICS) comply with cybersecurity standards and remain resilient to evolving cyber threats. While standards such as IEC 62443 and NIST provide structured guidance for securing industrial systems, translating these highlevel requirements into concrete and executable security tests remains a largely manual process. In practice, analysts must interpret heterogeneous standards, derive security controls, identify relevant adversarial behaviors, and design testing procedures for the target environment. This limits the repeatability and scalability of security assessments across industrial contexts. This paper presents a standards-driven approach that transforms cybersecurity requirements into executable adversary emulation procedures for ICS security assessment. The proposed framework extracts security controls from standards, aligns them with adversarial behaviors described in the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base for ICS, and generates environment-aware test actions executable through the MITRE CALDERA adversary emulation platform. An AIassisted pipeline supports the interpretation of requirements and the generation of test procedures while preserving human oversight and process traceability. By leveraging CALDERA as the execution layer, the approach decouples the assessment methodology from the target system, enabling the same adversary procedures to be applied across different environments such as virtual testbeds, digital twins, and operational systems. The approach is validated through two industrial case studies, demonstrating how standards-driven adversary emulation supports repeatable security assessments in heterogeneous ICS environments.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Moving Target Defense in Cyber-Physical Systems.
abstract: Cyber-physical power systems face coordinated false data injection attack (FDI) attacks that exploit the cyber measurement pipeline and knowledge of the power-flow Jacobian to bypass bad-data detection. Existing moving target defense (MTD) approaches address each layer in isolation, leaving a critical cross-layer seam that adaptive adversaries can exploit. This paper presents a unified, agentic artificial intelligence (AI)-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework that jointly optimizes physical MTD actions such as topology switching, flexible alternating current transmission system (FACTS) configuration, and distributed energy resource (DER) control with measurementcentric cyber-agility actions, including dynamic watermarking, adaptive scheduling, and estimator reconfiguration. A large language model (LLM) orchestrator, grounded via retrieval augmented generation (RAG) over domain threat knowledge, guides a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) network operating over a high-fidelity digital twin with crosslayer interdependency modeling. Preliminary results on the IEEE 14-bus system demonstrate improved FDI detection over physical-only and cyber-only baselines while maintaining frequency deviation within \pm 0.05 \text{Hz} , with full evaluation planned across IEEE 14, 39, 57, and 118-bus benchmarks.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: LLM4BP: A Collaborative LLM Framework for Insider-Resilient BPMN Workflows in Industrial Control Systems.
abstract: Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is widely adopted in industrial environments to describe operational workflows. However, these models are typically focused on functionality and efficiency, while cybersecurity controls, particularly those addressing insider threats, are rarely embedded at the modelling stage. This gap exposes process-driven systems to security risks such as privilege misuse, unauthorized task manipulation, and violations of segregation of duties. As a result, industrial workflows may remain vulnerable to malicious or negligent insiders despite existing system-level security mechanisms. This paper presents LLM4BP, a collaborative Large Language Model (LLM) framework for automated insider threat identification and security augmentation of BPMN workflows. LLM4BP employs a dual-LLM architecture in which one model identifies insider threat vectors within a BPMN process, while a second model validates the generated mitigations. The framework automatically injects explicit security control patterns, such as role separation, approval steps, and traceability mechanisms, directly into the BPMN while preserving structural and behavioural correctness. We evaluate LLM4BP on an industrial control system workflow, measuring threat detection coverage, structural impact using Relative Graph Edit Distance (RGED), and computational overhead. Experimental results show that LLM4BP can automatically integrate security controls with moderate structural modifications while preserving process behavior and maintaining acceptable performance overhead, demonstrating the feasibility of LLM-assisted security augmentation for industrial BPMN workflows.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Controller Placement in Hybrid SDN Networks: Classical Heuristics vs Quantum-inspired Optimization.
abstract: Software Defined Networking (SDN) has revolutionized network management by decoupling the control and data planes, yet optimizing controller placement within hybrid networks remains a complex challenge affecting latency and reliability. This work investigates the foundatioanl CPP (Controller Placemnet Problem) optimization problem by benchmarking classical algorithms, specifically Greedy Optimization and K-Medoids, against quantum-inspired QAOA (Quantum Approximation Optmization Algorithm) models using real-world topologies from the Internet Topology Zoo, including AT&T North America and ERNET India. Through extensive simulations involving randomly distributed SDN and legacy nodes (Non-SDN), we evaluated each approach based on average end-to-end latency, computational efficiency, and selection stability. The findings reveal that while Greedy Optimization provides the most effective classical performance, quantum-inspired methods offer competitive solutions for limited candidate sets, paving the way for future hybrid classical–quantum network architectures.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: CRISP: End-to-End Fingerprint Recognition Leveraging Hardware-Anchored Liveness Detection.
abstract: Modern fingerprint sensors remain critically vulnerable to presentation attacks (PA), as spoofs fabricated from everyday materials can successfully bypass both enrollment and authentication. Our evaluation of seven commercial devices confirms this urgent threat, highlighting the need for robust antispoofing mechanisms beyond software-only countermeasures. To address this challenge, we propose a robust fingerprint recognition system featuring CRISP, a dedicated processor for hardware-anchored liveness detection. By unifying a specialized sensing interface with a near-sensor AI processing engine, CRISP identifies the unique bioelectrical characteristics of live tissue in real time, even in interference-heavy industrial environments, within a single hardware unit. We validate the industrial feasibility of CRISP through non-intrusive parallel integration with a commercial pattern-matching sensor, demonstrating complete end-to-end operation within the Windows Hello application. The integrated system effectively rejects conductive spoofs in 0.82 seconds, providing a secure and reliable anti-spoofing framework for consumer biometric devices.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: AdROD: Adaptive Redundancy for Object Detection in Autonomous Driving.
abstract: Object detection is essential for real-time environmental recognition for autonomous driving systems. Recognition errors in autonomous driving can lead to catastrophic consequences. Therefore, a reliable architecture for making object detection systems tolerant to inference errors is necessary. This paper proposes AdROD, an adaptive redundancy technique for a real-time object detection system, aimed at reducing detection errors through redundancy while maintaining an affordable computational overhead. To reduce computational cost, AdROD dynamically adjusts the number of active detection models based on the uncertainty of detection results. By monitoring the confidence and agreement scores of detection results, AdROD includes additional models in the active set only when needed. We evaluate AdROD using a dataset collected from the CARLA autonomous driving simulator and demonstrate that the proposed method reduces computational costs by 77.8% compared to a static three-version redundant system, while maintaining comparable detection performance in terms of mAP and F1 score. AdROD effectively balances reliability and computational efficiency, making it a practical solution for real-time object detection in autonomous driving.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Threat-Oriented Digital Twinning for Security Evaluation of Autonomous Platforms.
abstract: Open, unclassified research on secure autonomy is constrained by limited access to operational platforms, contested communications infrastructure, and representative adversarial test conditions. This paper presents a threat-oriented digital twinning methodology for cybersecurity evaluation of learning-enabled autonomous platforms. The approach is instantiated as an open-source, modular twin of a representative autonomy stack with separated sensing, autonomy, and supervisory-control functions; confidence-gated multi-modal perception; explicit command and telemetry trust boundaries; and runtime hold-safe behavior. The contribution is methodological: a reproducible design pattern that translates threat analysis into observable, controllable tests for spoofing, replay, malformed-input injection, degraded sensing, and adversarial ML stress. Although the implemented proxy is ground based, the architecture is intentionally framed around stack elements shared with UAV and space systems, including constrained onboard compute, intermittent or high-latency links, probabilistic perception, and mission-critical recovery behavior. The result is an implementable research scaffold for dependable and secure autonomy studies across UAV and space domains.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: LaserTag: A Tool for Autonomous XAI-Guided Physical Adversarial Perturbations in Industrial Vision Pipelines.
abstract: We introduce LaserTag, an open-source toolchain for studying physical-world adversarial effects on industrial vision pipelines. The system couples lightweight classifiers with XAI methods and a reproducible pan–tilt laser actuation rig to identify salient image regions and probe them with controlled optical perturbations. Designed for dependability research, it supports interactive operation, automated logging, and repeatable experimentation. We evaluate LaserTag on three representative industrial controllers, highlighting practical vulnerabilities in vision-based status recognition. Rather than optimizing attacks, the toolchain provides an auditable testbed for autonomous XAI-guided targeting, surrogate-model transferability analysis, and countermeasure assessment. Experiments show that XAI-guided laser perturbations reliably induce both failure masking and spurious alarms, while several digital defenses—including color-channel suppression, highlight clipping, and laser inpainting—successfully restore correct predictions across both main and surrogate models. Code and models are released for reproducible research.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: SnipleyFuzz: Enhancing Black-Box Fuzzing of IoT Devices with Shapley-Based Priority Selection.
abstract: In recent years, the rapid development of the Internet of Things (IoT) has exposed a growing number of security vulnerabilities. Many existing testing approaches assume that firmware images are available, yet vendors rarely release them, making most techniques impractical in real-world settings. Consequently, firmware-independent black-box fuzzing is a more viable strategy, but current black-box fuzzers offer limited feedback and struggle with irregular protocols. We present SnipleyFuzz, a priority-based, response-oriented black-box fuzzing framework. SnipleyFuzz estimates snippet-level contributions from device responses and uses contextual multi-armed bandit (CMAB) scheduling to adapt the selection of message snippets during fuzzing. By replacing unavailable code coverage with response-centric signals, SnipleyFuzz enables protocol-agnostic, firmware-independent adaptive prioritization and cooperative mutation across message snippets. We implemented a prototype of SnipleyFuzz and evaluated it on six commercial IoT devices, discovering 48 unique crash-inducing test cases under black-box observation. Compared with Snipuzz and BooFuzz, SnipleyFuzz achieves higher response diversity, better response-space exploration efficiency, and more crash-inducing test cases in our experiments.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks
